intro: Five modules, one per AZ-104 skill area. Each has a study guide, slideshow, narrated lesson and worked exam scenario, aligned with the skills measured as of April 17, 2026.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-104

modules.title: Manage Azure identities and governance
modules.summary: Microsoft Entra users and groups, Azure RBAC, and the governance tools that keep subscriptions organized, compliant and on budget.

guide.html:
This domain is worth 20–25% of the exam. It has three parts: managing Microsoft Entra ID users and groups, controlling access to Azure resources with role-based access control (RBAC), and governing subscriptions with management groups, Azure Policy, locks, tags and cost tools.

Keep two permission systems separate in your head: Microsoft Entra roles (like User Administrator) manage the directory itself, while Azure RBAC roles (like Contributor) manage Azure resources.

guide.h: Users and groups in Microsoft Entra ID
guide.html:
Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is the identity service behind every Azure subscription. Users can be:

  • Members — created in your tenant, or synced from on-premises Active Directory with Microsoft Entra Connect.
  • Guests (external users) — invited through B2B collaboration. They sign in with their own organization's or personal account.

You can create users one at a time, or in bulk by uploading a CSV file in the portal. For bulk invites of guests there's a separate bulk invite template.

Groups come in two types: Security groups (to grant access) and Microsoft 365 groups (shared mailbox, calendar and files). Membership can be:

MembershipHow members are addedNotes
AssignedManually by an owner or adminSimple and static
Dynamic userAutomatically, by a rule such as user.department -eq "Sales"Requires Microsoft Entra ID P1
Dynamic deviceAutomatically, by device attributesSecurity groups only; requires P1

Licenses (such as Microsoft 365 or Entra ID P1/P2) can be assigned directly to users or, more efficiently, through group-based licensing, which requires P1. A user must have a usage location set before a license can be assigned.

Self-service password reset (SSPR) lets users reset forgotten passwords without the help desk. Key settings:

  • Scope: None, Selected (a group), or All users.
  • Number of methods required: 1 or 2.
  • Methods: Microsoft Authenticator, mobile phone, office phone, email, security questions and more.
  • Registration: you can require users to register when they next sign in, and to reconfirm their information every so many days.
  • Password writeback (for synced users) sends the new password back to on-premises AD.

Administrators always get SSPR with a stricter two-method policy and can't use security questions, regardless of what you configure for users.

guide.h: Azure RBAC: who can do what, where
guide.html:
A role assignment has three parts: a security principal (user, group, service principal or managed identity), a role definition (a set of allowed actions), and a scope.

Common built-in roles:

RoleCan manage resources?Can grant access?
OwnerYesYes
ContributorYesNo
ReaderView onlyNo
User Access AdministratorNoYes
Role Based Access Control AdministratorNoYes, with optional conditions limiting which roles can be assigned

Scopes, from broadest to narrowest: management group → subscription → resource group → resource. Assignments are inherited downward, and permissions are additive: a user gets the union of all their role assignments. Explicit deny assignments (created by features such as deployment stacks or managed applications) override allows.

Use Access control (IAM) → Check access on any resource to see a user's effective access and where each assignment comes from (direct, group, or inherited).

guide.h: Management groups, subscriptions and resource groups
guide.html:
Management groups sit above subscriptions so you can apply RBAC and Azure Policy to many subscriptions at once. Every tenant has a single root management group. The hierarchy supports up to six levels below the root (not counting subscriptions), and each subscription or management group has exactly one parent.

A subscription is a billing and management boundary. You can move subscriptions between management groups, transfer billing ownership, and set subscription-level budgets.

A resource group is a logical container. Each resource lives in exactly one resource group, though resources can be in different regions from their group. Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it. Many resources can be moved between resource groups and subscriptions (use the validate step first); the resource ID changes after a move.

Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules and enforces standards. The building blocks:

  • Policy definition — a rule in JSON, such as "allowed locations".
  • Initiative (policy set) — a group of definitions, such as a regulatory standard.
  • Assignment — applies a definition or initiative to a scope, with optional exclusions and parameters.

Important effects:

EffectWhat it does
DenyBlocks non-compliant create or update requests
AuditAllows the request but marks the resource non-compliant
Append / ModifyAdds or changes properties or tags during create/update
DeployIfNotExistsDeploys a related resource (for example, a diagnostic setting) if missing
AuditIfNotExistsFlags resources that lack a related resource
DenyActionBlocks specific actions, such as deleting a resource

Policies with Modify or DeployIfNotExists need a managed identity on the assignment, and existing resources are fixed with a remediation task. New assignments can take up to about 30 minutes to start evaluating.

Locks protect resources from accidental changes, even by Owners:

  • CanNotDelete (Delete in the portal) — users can read and modify, but not delete.
  • ReadOnly — users can only read. This can block operations you might not expect, such as listing storage account keys (a POST action).

Locks are inherited by child resources. Only roles with Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* permissions, such as Owner and User Access Administrator, can create or remove them.

Tags are name–value pairs (for example CostCenter=Finance) used for organization and cost reporting. Each resource, resource group or subscription can have up to 50 tags. Tags are not inherited automatically; use Azure Policy (for example, "Inherit a tag from the resource group") to apply them.

• Cost analysis shows spending by service, resource group, tag and more.
  • Budgets send alerts when actual or forecast spending crosses thresholds. Budgets don't stop resources by themselves, but alerts can trigger an action group (for example, an Automation runbook).
  • Cost alerts include budget alerts, credit alerts and department spending quota alerts.
  • Azure Advisor gives recommendations in five categories: cost, security, reliability, operational excellence and performance — for example, resizing or shutting down underused VMs.
  • Savings options include reservations, savings plans, Azure Hybrid Benefit and Spot VMs.

guide.h: Worked scenario: least-privilege access for an auditor
guide.html:
Scenario: An external auditor needs to inspect Azure resource settings in one production resource group for a short review. They must not be able to change resources or administer the directory.

Pause and decide: Which identity, role and scope meet the requirement with the narrowest practical access?

Recommended design

  1. Invite the auditor as a Microsoft Entra guest using B2B collaboration.
  2. Add the guest to a dedicated security group used for the review.
  3. Assign the Azure RBAC Reader role to that group at the target resource-group scope.
  4. After the review, remove the role assignment or group membership and retire the guest account according to the organization's access process.

Why this fits: Reader grants control-plane visibility without resource changes. Resource-group scope keeps the assignment inside the review boundary; it doesn't grant a Microsoft Entra directory role or access to sibling resource groups. Check the exact data-plane permissions separately if the auditor also needs to read data stored inside a service.

Microsoft Learn: Azure RBAC

tips: If a question asks who can assign roles but not manage resources, the answer is usually User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator.
Dynamic groups and group-based licensing both need Microsoft Entra ID P1.
Locks beat RBAC: an Owner can't delete a resource with a CanNotDelete lock until the lock is removed.
Tags are not inherited unless Azure Policy applies them.
A budget alerts; it doesn't shut anything down on its own.
terms: Security principal
An identity that can be granted access: user, group, service principal or managed identity.
Scope
Where a role or policy applies: management group, subscription, resource group or resource.
Initiative
A collection of policy definitions assigned together.
Remediation task
Brings existing resources into compliance for Modify and DeployIfNotExists policies.
B2B collaboration
Inviting external users as guests who sign in with their own credentials.

slides.title: Manage Azure identities and governance
bullets: Users, groups and licenses in Microsoft Entra ID
Governance: management groups, Policy, locks, tags and costs
script: Welcome to module one of the AZ-104 course: managing Azure identities and governance.
This domain is worth twenty to twenty-five percent of the exam, so it's one of the biggest.

We'll cover users, groups and licenses in Microsoft Entra ID, then how Azure role-based access control works, and finally the governance tools that keep subscriptions organized, compliant and on budget.

slides.title: Two permission systems
bullets: Microsoft Entra roles manage the directory: users, groups, licenses
Azure RBAC roles manage resources: VMs, storage, networks
A Global Administrator isn't automatically an Azure Owner
script: Before anything else, separate two permission systems.
Microsoft Entra roles, like User Administrator, control the directory itself: users, groups and licenses.
Azure RBAC roles, like Owner and Contributor, control Azure resources such as virtual machines and storage accounts.
Exam questions often hinge on picking the role from the right system.

slides.title: Users: members and guests
bullets: Members are created in the tenant or synced from on-premises AD
Bulk create or invite users with a CSV upload
script: Microsoft Entra ID has two kinds of users.
Members are created in your tenant, or synchronized from on-premises Active Directory using Microsoft Entra Connect.
Guests are external users you invite with B2B collaboration. They redeem the invitation and sign in with their own account.
For lots of users at once, the portal lets you upload a CSV file to bulk create or bulk invite.

slides.title: Groups and membership types
bullets: Security groups grant access; Microsoft 365 groups add collaboration
script: Groups come in two types. Security groups are used to grant access. Microsoft 365 groups add a shared mailbox, calendar and files.
Membership can be assigned manually, or dynamic.
A dynamic rule, like the one on screen, adds and removes users automatically based on attributes such as department.
Remember that dynamic membership requires a Microsoft Entra ID P1 license.

slides.title: Licenses
bullets: Group licensing auto-assigns as members join
script: Licenses can be assigned to individual users, but group-based licensing is easier at scale. Members get the license automatically when they join the group.
Group-based licensing requires P1.
One common gotcha: a user needs a usage location set before a license can be assigned.

slides.title: Self-service password reset
bullets: Admins always use a stricter two-method policy
script: Self-service password reset lets users reset their own passwords.
You choose the scope: nobody, a selected group, or all users. And you choose whether one or two methods are required, such as the Authenticator app, phone or email.
Administrators are treated differently. They always get a stricter two-method policy, whatever you configure.
For users synced from on-premises, enable password writeback so the new password reaches Active Directory.

slides.title: Azure RBAC role assignments
bullets: Who: user, group, service principal or managed identity
script: Every Azure RBAC role assignment answers three questions.
Who: the security principal, which can be a user, group, service principal or managed identity.
What: the role definition, which lists the allowed actions.
And where: the scope the assignment applies to.

slides.title: Built-in roles to know
bullets: Contributor: manage everything, but can't grant access
script: Four built-in roles appear constantly on the exam.
Owner can do everything, including granting access to others.
Contributor can create and manage resources but can't grant access.
Reader can only view.

And User Access Administrator can manage access, but not the resources themselves. The newer Role Based Access Control Administrator role is similar, with optional conditions that limit which roles it can assign.

slides.title: Scopes and inheritance
bullets: Use Check access to see effective access
script: Scopes form a hierarchy: management group, subscription, resource group, then resource.
A role assigned at a higher scope is inherited by everything below it.
Permissions add up, so a user gets the union of all their assignments, whether direct or through groups.
Deny assignments are the exception: they block actions even if a role allows them.
To troubleshoot, open Access control and use Check access to see where someone's permissions come from.

slides.title: Management groups
bullets: Organize subscriptions for policy and access at scale
Up to six levels deep below the root
script: Management groups sit above subscriptions.
Assign a policy or role to a management group, and every subscription below inherits it.
Each tenant has one root management group, and the tree can go six levels deep below it.
A subscription can only have one parent at a time, but you can move it.

slides.title: Azure Policy building blocks
bullets: Compliance shows in the Policy dashboard
script: Azure Policy enforces standards across your environment.
A definition is a single rule, like allowed locations. An initiative groups several definitions together.
An assignment applies a definition or initiative to a scope, with parameters and optional exclusions.
Results show up as compliance data on the Policy dashboard.

slides.title: Policy effects
script: The effect decides what a policy does.
Deny blocks a non-compliant create or update. Audit lets it through but marks the resource non-compliant.
Modify changes properties or tags, and DeployIfNotExists deploys a related resource, such as a diagnostic setting.
Those two need a managed identity on the assignment, and existing resources are fixed with a remediation task.

slides.title: Resource locks

items.d: Blocks all changes, even some reads like listing keys

script: Locks protect critical resources from accidents.
A CanNotDelete lock allows changes but blocks deletion. A ReadOnly lock blocks changes entirely.
Locks apply to everyone, even Owners, until someone with lock permissions removes them.
Watch out: ReadOnly can block operations that sound like reads, such as listing storage account keys.

slides.title: Tags
bullets: Use Policy to inherit or require tags
script: Tags are name and value pairs you attach to resources, resource groups and subscriptions.
They're great for cost reporting and organizing resources.
The key exam fact: tags are not inherited automatically. If resources should get their resource group's tags, use an Azure Policy such as inherit a tag from the resource group.

slides.title: Managing costs
bullets: Budgets alert on actual or forecast spend
Reservations, savings plans and Hybrid Benefit cut costs
script: For costs, start with cost analysis to see where the money goes.
Budgets alert you when actual or forecast spending crosses a threshold. They don't stop resources on their own, but an action group can run automation.
Azure Advisor recommends savings, such as resizing or shutting down underused virtual machines.
And reservations, savings plans and Azure Hybrid Benefit can lower costs for steady workloads.

slides.title: Scenario: Give an external auditor read access
bullets: An auditor is outside the tenant
They need to inspect resources in one production resource group
They must not change resources or administer the directory
Pause and choose the identity, role and scope
script: A company has invited an external auditor to review the Azure resources in one production resource group. The auditor needs to inspect configuration, but must not make changes or administer the directory. Pause the lesson and choose the right identity, role and scope before moving on.

slides.title: Solution: guest identity, Reader role, resource-group scope
bullets: Invite the auditor as an Entra guest
Add the guest to a dedicated security group
Assign Azure RBAC Reader to the group at the target resource group
Remove access when the review ends
script: Use Microsoft Entra B2B to invite the auditor as a guest. Put the guest in a dedicated security group, then assign the Azure RBAC Reader role to that group at the target resource-group scope. Reader lets the auditor inspect Azure resource settings without changing them. The resource-group scope avoids granting access to sibling groups. Reader is a control-plane role, so check data-plane access separately if the audit also includes stored data. Remove the assignment or group membership when the review is complete.

slides.title: Module 1 recap
bullets: Entra roles manage identities; RBAC manages resources
Dynamic groups and group licensing need P1
Policy enforces, locks protect, tags organize
script: Let's recap module one.
Entra roles manage identities, while Azure RBAC manages resources.
Dynamic groups and group-based licensing require P1.
RBAC assignments are inherited down the hierarchy and add up.
Azure Policy enforces rules, locks protect resources, and tags organize them.
And for costs, budgets alert while Advisor recommends.
Next, read the study guide or try the practice questions for this domain.

modules.title: Implement and manage storage
modules.summary: Storage accounts, redundancy, access control with keys, SAS and identity, Azure Files and Blob features like tiers, lifecycle, versioning and soft delete.

guide.html: This domain is worth 15–20% of the exam. It covers securing access to storage, configuring storage accounts (redundancy, replication, encryption, tools), and Azure Files and Blob Storage features.

A storage account is a unique namespace (https://<name>.blob.core.windows.net) that holds four data services: Blob (objects), Files (SMB/NFS shares), Queue (messages) and Table (NoSQL key–attribute data).

Account typeUse it for
Standard general-purpose v2Most scenarios: blobs, files, queues, tables. The default choice.
Premium block blobsLow-latency, high-transaction blob workloads
Premium file sharesHigh-performance SMB and NFS shares
Premium page blobsPage blobs only, such as unmanaged disks

Account names must be 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, and globally unique.

OptionCopiesProtects against
LRS3 in one datacenterDisk and rack failures
ZRS3 across availability zonesA datacenter (zone) outage
GRSLRS + 3 in the paired regionA regional outage
GZRSZRS + 3 in the paired regionZone and regional outages

Add RA- (RA-GRS, RA-GZRS) for read access to the secondary region at any time through a -secondary endpoint. Otherwise the secondary is only readable after a failover. An unplanned customer-managed failover makes the secondary the new primary, and the account becomes LRS until you reconfigure geo-redundancy. A planned failover swaps regions and keeps geo-redundancy.

Premium file shares and premium block blobs support only LRS and ZRS.

• Access keys — two keys give full access to the account. Rotate one at a time; store them in Key Vault. You can disable Shared Key authorization entirely.
  • Shared access signatures (SAS) — tokens granting limited permissions, for a limited time, optionally from specific IPs and over HTTPS only.
    • User delegation SAS: signed with Microsoft Entra credentials; Blob only; the most secure.
    • Service SAS: signed with the account key, for one service.
    • Account SAS: signed with the account key, for one or more services.
  • Stored access policies — defined on a container (or share, queue, table). A service SAS linked to a policy can be revoked by changing or deleting the policy. Up to 5 per container.
  • Microsoft Entra ID + RBAC — roles like Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor grant data access. Note that Contributor and Owner are control-plane roles; they reach data only through the account keys.
  • Identity-based access for Azure Files — SMB shares can use on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Kerberos, with share-level RBAC roles (Storage File Data SMB Share Reader/Contributor/Elevated Contributor) plus NTFS permissions.

To revoke an ad hoc SAS (one without a stored access policy), you must regenerate the key that signed it.

Storage firewall settings let you allow access only from selected VNets (with service endpoints) and IP ranges, or disable public access and use private endpoints. Trusted Microsoft services can be allowed as an exception.

All data is encrypted at rest with 256-bit AES (Storage Service Encryption). Keys can be Microsoft-managed or customer-managed in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM. Encryption scopes let you use different keys per container or blob. Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer and must be enabled at account creation.

Azure Storage Explorer is a desktop GUI for browsing and managing storage. The portal also has a built-in Storage browser.

AzCopy is a command-line tool for copying data at scale:

azcopy login
azcopy copy "C:\data" "https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/backup?<SAS>" --recursive
azcopy sync "C:\data" "https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/backup" --delete-destination=true

AzCopy authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID (azcopy login) or a SAS token. Copies between storage accounts happen server-to-server.

Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs from a source container to a destination container in another account. It requires blob versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source.

• Fully managed file shares over SMB (port 445) and NFS (premium only).
  • Tiers: Premium (SSD), and Transaction optimized, Hot and Cool on standard storage.
  • Snapshots are read-only, point-in-time copies of a share; Windows users can see them as Previous Versions.
  • Soft delete for shares keeps deleted shares for 1–365 days.
  • Azure File Sync caches shares on Windows Servers with cloud tiering. Components: Storage Sync Service → sync group → cloud endpoint (the share) and server endpoints (paths on registered servers).

If clients can't mount an SMB share, check that outbound TCP 445 isn't blocked by the ISP or firewall.

Access tiers for block blobs:

TierMinimum retentionNotes
Hot—Frequent access; highest storage cost, lowest access cost
Cool30 daysInfrequent access
Cold90 daysRare access, but still online
Archive180 daysOffline; rehydrate to Hot, Cool or Cold first (up to 15 hours at standard priority)

Deleting or moving a blob before the minimum period incurs an early deletion charge.

  • Lifecycle management — JSON rules that move blobs to cooler tiers or delete them based on age (last modified, created, or last accessed with access tracking enabled). Rules run once a day.
  • Blob soft delete — recovers deleted blobs and snapshots for 1–365 days. Container soft delete does the same for containers.
  • Versioning — automatically keeps previous versions whenever a blob is overwritten or deleted.
  • Snapshots — manual read-only copies of a blob at a point in time.
  • Point-in-time restore — restores block blobs to an earlier state; needs versioning, change feed and soft delete.
  • Immutable storage — time-based retention or legal hold policies for WORM (write once, read many) compliance.

guide.h: Worked scenario: revocable, read-only container access
guide.html:
Scenario: A contractor needs temporary read access to a Blob Storage container while migrating data. The access should be limited to the required operations and revocable without rotating the storage account keys.

Pause and decide: Which SAS type supports a stored access policy, and what should the policy restrict?

Recommended design

  1. Create a stored access policy on the container with the required start and expiry times and only the needed permissions, such as read and list.
  2. Create a service SAS for that container that references the policy. Require HTTPS and share the token through an approved secret-sharing channel.
  3. If access must end early, change or remove the stored access policy to revoke the service SAS.

Exam distinction: A user delegation SAS is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials and is a strong default for Blob access, but it must be ad hoc; it cannot reference a stored access policy. If policy-based revocation is a requirement, the service SAS is the matching answer. Treat either SAS as a bearer secret.

Microsoft Learn: Shared access signatures

tips: Need to read from the secondary region without failover? Pick an RA- option (RA-GRS or RA-GZRS).
Survive a zone outage but stay in one region: ZRS.
The way to revoke a SAS without regenerating keys is a stored access policy.
Object replication needs versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source.
Archive blobs must be rehydrated before they can be read.
terms: SAS
Shared access signature: a token granting limited, time-bound access to storage resources.
Stored access policy
Container-level policy a service SAS can reference, so the SAS can be changed or revoked.
Rehydration
Moving a blob out of the Archive tier so it can be read.
Cloud tiering
Azure File Sync feature that keeps hot files local and cold files only in Azure.
Change feed
An ordered log of changes to blobs in an account.

slides.title: Implement and manage storage
bullets: Securing access: keys, SAS and identity
Azure Files and Blob Storage features
script: Welcome to module two: implementing and managing storage.
This domain is worth fifteen to twenty percent of the exam.
We'll cover storage accounts and redundancy, how to secure access with keys, shared access signatures and identities, and then the features of Azure Files and Blob Storage.

slides.title: One account, four services
script: A storage account is a single namespace that holds four services.
Blob storage holds unstructured objects such as images, backups and logs.
Azure Files provides managed SMB and NFS file shares.
Queues pass messages between application components, and Table storage holds simple NoSQL data.
For most scenarios, choose a standard general-purpose v2 account.

slides.title: Account types
bullets: Premium file shares: fast SMB and NFS
script: There are four account types.
Standard general-purpose v2 is the default and supports every service.
Premium accounts use SSDs and are specialized: block blobs for low latency, file shares for high-performance SMB and NFS, and page blobs.
Storage account names must be three to twenty-four characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, and globally unique.

slides.title: Redundancy options
script: Redundancy decides how many copies of your data exist and where.
Locally redundant storage keeps three copies in one datacenter.
Zone redundant storage spreads three copies across availability zones, so it survives a zone outage.
Geo-redundant storage adds three more copies in the paired region, and geo-zone-redundant storage combines zones and a paired region.

slides.title: Read access and failover
bullets: RA-GRS / RA-GZRS: read the secondary any time
Without RA, the secondary is readable only after failover
After unplanned failover, the account becomes LRS
script: Geo-replication to the secondary region is asynchronous.
With plain GRS, you can't read from the secondary until a failover happens.
If you add read access, as in RA-GRS or RA-GZRS, applications can read from the secondary endpoint at any time.
After an unplanned customer-managed failover, the account becomes locally redundant until you reconfigure geo-redundancy.

slides.title: Access keys and SAS
bullets: Two access keys = full access; rotate one at a time
User delegation SAS: signed with Entra ID
Service and account SAS: signed with a key
script: Each storage account has two access keys that grant full access. Rotate them one at a time so apps can switch over without downtime.
A shared access signature grants limited permissions for a limited time.
The user delegation SAS is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials and is the most secure option, but it only works for Blob storage.
Service and account SAS tokens are signed with an account key.

slides.title: Stored access policies
bullets: Defined on a container, share, queue or table
A service SAS can reference the policy
Change or delete the policy to revoke the SAS
script: A SAS is valid until it expires, so how do you revoke one early?
If the SAS is ad hoc, you have to regenerate the key that signed it, which breaks everything else using that key.
The better approach is a stored access policy on the container. A service SAS that references the policy can be revoked just by changing or deleting the policy.
Each container can have up to five stored access policies.

slides.title: Identity-based access
bullets: Storage Blob Data roles grant data access
Contributor and Owner manage the account, not data
Azure Files supports AD DS, Entra Domain Services and Entra Kerberos
script: Microsoft Entra ID is the recommended way to authorize data access.
Assign data roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Storage Blob Data Contributor.
Don't confuse these with Owner and Contributor, which manage the account itself.
For Azure Files over SMB, you can use on-premises Active Directory, Entra Domain Services or Entra Kerberos, with share-level roles combined with NTFS permissions.

slides.title: Network access and encryption
bullets: Firewall: selected VNets and IP ranges
Encryption at rest is always on (AES-256)
script: By default, a storage account accepts connections from any network.
The storage firewall can restrict access to selected virtual networks, using service endpoints, and specific IP ranges.
For fully private access, use a private endpoint, which gives the account a private IP address in your virtual network.
Data is always encrypted at rest. You can use Microsoft-managed keys or your own customer-managed keys stored in Key Vault.

slides.title: Moving data with AzCopy
bullets: Authenticate with azcopy login or a SAS
script: AzCopy is the command-line tool for moving data into, out of and between storage accounts.
Authenticate with azcopy login for Microsoft Entra ID, or append a SAS token to the URL.
Use copy for one-time transfers and sync to keep a destination matched to a source.
If you prefer a graphical tool, use Azure Storage Explorer or the Storage browser in the portal.

slides.title: Object replication
bullets: Copies block blobs to another account asynchronously
Good for latency and data distribution
script: Object replication copies block blobs from a container in one account to a container in another.
It's asynchronous, and you control which blobs replicate with rules and prefix filters.
The prerequisites are a classic exam question: blob versioning on both accounts, and change feed on the source account.

slides.title: Azure Files
bullets: SMB on port 445; NFS on premium
Azure File Sync caches shares on Windows Server
Cloud tiering keeps hot files local
script: Azure Files offers fully managed shares over SMB, and NFS on premium accounts.
If a client can't mount a share, check whether outbound port four forty-five is blocked.
Snapshots and soft delete protect your data from mistakes.

Azure File Sync caches a share on Windows Servers. A sync group has one cloud endpoint, the share, and server endpoints on registered servers. Cloud tiering keeps only frequently used files on the local disk.

slides.title: Blob access tiers
script: Block blobs have four access tiers.
Hot is for frequent access. Cool and Cold are cheaper to store but cost more to read, with minimum retention periods of thirty and ninety days.
Archive is the cheapest, but it's offline. You must rehydrate a blob to an online tier before reading it, which can take up to fifteen hours at standard priority.
Moving or deleting blobs early incurs an early deletion charge.

slides.title: Lifecycle management
bullets: JSON rules move or delete blobs by age
Based on modified, created or last accessed time
Filter by prefix or blob index tags
script: Lifecycle management automates tiering.
You write rules, like the one on screen, that move blobs to cool after thirty days, archive after ninety, and delete after a year.
Rules can use the last modified time, the creation time, or the last access time if access tracking is on.
Policies run once a day, so changes aren't instant.

slides.title: Data protection for blobs
bullets: Soft delete for blobs and containers (1–365 days)
script: Several features protect blob data.
Soft delete lets you recover deleted blobs or containers for one to three hundred sixty-five days.
Versioning automatically keeps the previous version whenever a blob is overwritten.
Point-in-time restore can roll back block blobs to an earlier state.
And immutable storage enforces write once, read many with legal holds or time-based retention.

slides.title: Scenario: temporary access for a migration contractor
bullets: The contractor needs read-only access to one blob container
Access must expire after the migration
You need a way to revoke it early
Pause and choose the SAS type
script: A contractor needs temporary read-only access to one Blob Storage container for a migration. The access should expire, and the storage team must be able to revoke it early without rotating account keys. Pause and choose which SAS type and control meet those requirements.

slides.title: Solution: service SAS tied to a stored access policy
bullets: Create a container stored access policy with narrow permissions and dates
Issue a service SAS that references the policy
Require HTTPS and protect the token as a secret
Change or delete the policy to revoke associated SAS tokens
script: For policy-based revocation, use a service SAS associated with a stored access policy on the container. Limit the policy to the required read and list operations and the migration window. Require HTTPS and share the SAS URI securely because anyone holding it can use its permissions. If the task instead asks for a Microsoft Entra signed Blob SAS without policy-based revocation, consider a user delegation SAS. User delegation SAS tokens are ad hoc and cannot use a stored access policy.

slides.title: Module 2 recap
bullets: GPv2 is the default account type
ZRS for zones, GRS for regions, RA- to read the secondary
Stored access policies make SAS revocable
Object replication needs versioning and change feed
script: Let's recap module two.
Standard general-purpose v2 is the default account type.
Pick ZRS to survive a zone outage, GRS or GZRS for a regional outage, and an RA option to read the secondary at any time.
Stored access policies let you revoke a SAS.
Object replication requires versioning and change feed.
And archived blobs must be rehydrated before you can read them.
Next, review the study guide or practice storage questions.

modules.title: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
modules.summary: ARM templates and Bicep, virtual machines and their availability options, scale sets, containers (ACR, ACI, Container Apps) and App Service.

guide.html: This domain is worth 20–25% of the exam. It covers automating deployments with ARM templates and Bicep, virtual machines, containers, and Azure App Service.

Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management layer for Azure. Infrastructure as code lets you deploy the same environment repeatedly.

  • ARM templates are JSON files with $schema, contentVersion, parameters, variables, resources and outputs.
  • Bicep is a simpler language that compiles to ARM JSON. Use az bicep decompile to convert JSON to Bicep and az bicep build for the reverse.
  • Deployments are idempotent: running the same template again produces the same result.
  • Deployment modes: Incremental (default) adds or updates resources and leaves others alone; Complete deletes resources in the resource group that aren't in the template.
  • Use what-if to preview changes before deploying.
  • You can export a template from a resource group, a resource, or the deployment history.
param location string = resourceGroup().location
resource sa 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-05-01' = {
  name: 'stcontoso${uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)}'
  location: location
  sku: { name: 'Standard_LRS' }
  kind: 'StorageV2'
}
az deployment group create -g rg1 --template-file main.bicep --parameters env=prod

• Sizes are grouped into families: B (burstable), D (general purpose), E (memory optimized), F (compute optimized), L (storage), N (GPU) and more. Resizing usually restarts the VM; if the size isn't available on the current hardware cluster, deallocate first.
  • Disks: OS disk, optional temporary disk (data is lost on deallocation or redeploy), and managed data disks. Types: Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk.
  • Encryption: managed disks always use server-side encryption. Encryption at host also encrypts temp disks and caches, end to end. Azure Disk Encryption uses BitLocker or DM-Crypt inside the guest OS.
  • Moving a VM to another resource group or subscription moves it and its dependent resources; the VM keeps running. Use Azure Resource Mover to move to another region.
  • Use VM extensions (such as Custom Script Extension) to configure VMs after deployment.
  • Stopped (deallocated) VMs don't incur compute charges; Stopped from inside the OS still does.

OptionProtects againstSLA (two or more VMs)
Availability setRack and host failures, planned maintenance (fault and update domains)99.95%
Availability zonesA whole datacenter failure99.99%

An availability set has up to 3 fault domains (separate power and network) and up to 20 update domains (rebooted one at a time during maintenance). A VM can only be placed in an availability set when it's created.

Virtual Machine Scale Sets run identical, load-balanced VMs and autoscale on metrics like CPU or on a schedule. Flexible orchestration (the default) supports mixing VM sizes and spreading across zones and fault domains.

ServiceWhat it isWhen to choose it
Azure Container Registry (ACR)A private registry for container imagesStore and manage images; SKUs: Basic, Standard, Premium (geo-replication, private link)
Azure Container Instances (ACI)Run containers on demand without serversSimple tasks, batch jobs, quick tests
Azure Container AppsServerless container platform built on KubernetesMicroservices and APIs that need scaling (including to zero), revisions and ingress
  • ACI container groups share a lifecycle, network and storage — like a Kubernetes pod. Restart policies: Always, OnFailure, Never.
  • Container Apps scale with KEDA rules (HTTP traffic, CPU, queue length) and support revisions for traffic splitting.
  • To let a service pull from ACR, give its managed identity the AcrPull role.

• An App Service plan defines the region, OS, VM size and count. All apps in a plan share those resources.
  • Tiers: Free and Shared (dev/test), Basic (custom domains and SSL), Standard (autoscale, deployment slots, backups), Premium (more scale and slots), Isolated (an App Service Environment in your VNet).
  • Scale up changes the tier/size; scale out adds instances, manually or with autoscale rules.
  • Deployment slots (Standard and above) run staging versions; swap to production with warm-up and instant rollback. Settings marked deployment slot setting stay with the slot.
  • Custom domains need a DNS record (CNAME or A) plus a TXT record (asuid) to verify ownership. TLS certificates can be free App Service managed certificates, imported from Key Vault, or uploaded.
  • Backups can be automatic or custom (custom backups need a storage account). Networking: VNet integration for outbound calls to private resources; private endpoints for private inbound access.

guide.h: Worked scenario: stage and safely release an App Service update
guide.html:
Scenario: A team needs to validate a new web app version before users receive it. The production app has environment-specific settings, and the team needs a straightforward way to return to the previous version if validation fails.

Pause and decide: Which App Service feature provides a separate staging environment, and which settings must stay with each slot?

Recommended release path

  1. Use an App Service plan that supports deployment slots, such as Standard or higher, then deploy the candidate to a staging slot.
  2. Mark environment-specific app settings and connection strings as deployment slot settings so they remain with the intended slot during a swap.
  3. Warm up and validate the staging slot, then swap it with production.
  4. If the new version fails after release, swap back to restore the previous production version, then investigate in staging.

Keep the concepts separate: A slot swap promotes an app deployment; it doesn't replace backups. For a custom domain, configure DNS ownership and a certificate binding separately. App Service VNet integration is for outbound access; a private endpoint provides private inbound access.

Microsoft Learn: App Service deployment slots

tips: Complete mode deletes resources not in the template; Incremental (the default) doesn't.
Availability set = 99.95% (racks); availability zones = 99.99% (datacenters).
You can't add an existing VM to an availability set; you must recreate it.
Deployment slots and autoscale need at least the Standard App Service tier.
Temporary disk data is lost when a VM is deallocated, resized to new hardware, or redeployed.
terms: Idempotent
Running the same deployment repeatedly produces the same result.
Fault domain
A group of hardware sharing power and network; VMs in different fault domains survive rack failures.
Update domain
A group of VMs rebooted together during planned maintenance.
Container group
In ACI, containers scheduled together sharing network and storage.
Slot swap
Exchanging a staging slot with production, with warm-up and easy rollback.

slides.title: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
bullets: Virtual machines, availability and scale sets
script: Welcome to module three: deploying and managing Azure compute resources.
This domain is worth twenty to twenty-five percent of the exam.
We'll start with infrastructure as code using ARM templates and Bicep, then cover virtual machines and availability, and finish with containers and App Service.

slides.title: Infrastructure as code
bullets: Bicep: simpler syntax, compiles to ARM JSON
script: Azure Resource Manager handles every deployment in Azure, whether you use the portal, the CLI or code.
ARM templates describe resources in JSON. Bicep describes the same thing with much simpler syntax and compiles to ARM JSON.
Deployments are idempotent, so running the same template twice gives the same result.
Use what-if to preview what a deployment will change before you run it.

slides.title: Template structure
script: An ARM template has a standard structure.
Parameters are values you supply at deployment time, like an environment name.
Variables hold values you reuse inside the template.
Resources list what to deploy, and outputs return values, such as an IP address, after deployment.
You can also export a template from an existing resource group to start from what's already deployed.

slides.title: Deployment modes
bullets: Complete: delete what isn't in the template
Deploy with CLI, PowerShell, portal or pipelines

items.d: Existing extra resources are left alone
Extra resources in the group are deleted

script: Resource group deployments run in one of two modes.
Incremental, the default, adds and updates the resources in the template and leaves everything else alone.
Complete mode makes the resource group match the template exactly, deleting anything that isn't in it.
That difference shows up on the exam, so remember which mode deletes.

slides.title: Virtual machine basics
bullets: Size families: B, D, E, F, L, N…
script: Virtual machine sizes are grouped into families, such as B for burstable, D for general purpose, E for memory and F for compute.
Changing the size restarts the VM. If the new size isn't available on the current hardware, you'll need to deallocate it first.
Only a deallocated VM stops compute charges. Shutting down from inside the operating system doesn't.
Extensions, like the Custom Script Extension, configure software after deployment.

slides.title: Disks and encryption
bullets: OS disk, temporary disk, data disks
Temp disk data is lost on deallocation
Encryption at host: end-to-end, including temp disk
Azure Disk Encryption: BitLocker or DM-Crypt in the guest
script: Each VM has an OS disk, often a temporary disk, and optional data disks.
Never store important data on the temporary disk. It's wiped when the VM is deallocated or redeployed.
Managed disks are always encrypted at rest on the server side.
Encryption at host extends that encryption to temporary disks and caches. Azure Disk Encryption is different: it uses BitLocker or DM-Crypt inside the guest operating system.

slides.title: Moving VMs
bullets: Move between resource groups or subscriptions
Resource IDs change after a move
script: You can move a VM to another resource group or subscription. Its dependent resources, like disks and network interfaces, need to move with it.
To move a VM to a different region, use Azure Resource Mover, or Azure Site Recovery.
Remember that the resource ID changes after a move, so update any scripts that reference it.

slides.title: Availability sets vs zones
bullets: Set only when the VM is created
script: For high availability, run two or more VMs.
An availability set spreads them across fault domains, which have separate power and network, and update domains, which reboot at different times. That gives a 99.95 percent SLA.
Availability zones place VMs in physically separate datacenters for a 99.99 percent SLA.
You choose the availability option when creating the VM. You can't add an existing VM to an availability set.

slides.title: Fault and update domains
bullets: One update domain reboots at a time
script: Inside an availability set, fault domains are groups of hardware that share power and networking. There can be up to three.
Update domains are groups that Azure reboots together during planned maintenance. There can be up to twenty.
Spread VMs across them, and a single rack failure or maintenance event won't take down the whole application.

slides.title: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
script: Virtual Machine Scale Sets run a group of identical VMs behind a load balancer.
Autoscale adds instances when a metric, like CPU, crosses a threshold, and removes them when demand drops. You can also scale on a schedule.
Flexible orchestration is the default. It supports mixing VM sizes and spreading instances across zones and fault domains.

slides.title: Container options
bullets: ACI: run a container fast, no servers
script: Azure Container Registry stores your private container images. The Premium tier adds geo-replication and private link.
Azure Container Instances runs a container on demand without managing servers, which is perfect for simple tasks and batch jobs.
Azure Container Apps is a serverless platform for microservices, with autoscaling, scale to zero, revisions and ingress.
To pull images from the registry, give the service's managed identity the AcrPull role.

slides.title: ACI and Container Apps details
bullets: ACI container groups share network and storage
script: In Container Instances, a container group is a set of containers that share a lifecycle, network and storage, much like a Kubernetes pod.
Restart policies control what happens when containers exit: always, on failure, or never.
Container Apps scale using KEDA rules, based on HTTP traffic, CPU or queue length.
Revisions let you run multiple versions and split traffic between them.

slides.title: App Service plans
bullets: Plan = region, OS, size and instance count
Apps in a plan share resources
Scale up: bigger tier; scale out: more instances
script: An App Service plan defines the compute your web apps run on: the region, operating system, size and number of instances.
All apps in the same plan share those resources.
Scaling up moves to a bigger tier or size. Scaling out adds instances.
Autoscale and deployment slots need at least the Standard tier.

slides.title: Deployment slots
bullets: Swap after warm-up; swap back to restore the previous version
Slot settings stay with the slot
script: Deployment slots are live apps with their own host names.
Deploy to a staging slot, test it, then swap it with production. Azure warms up the instances first, so there's no downtime.
Deploy to a staging slot, validate it, then swap it with production. The swap warms up the target before routing traffic, which helps reduce disruption; validate the result in your own app.
App settings marked as deployment slot settings stay with their slot instead of moving during a swap.

slides.title: Domains, TLS, backup and networking
bullets: Custom domain: CNAME or A + TXT asuid record
TLS: managed certificate, Key Vault or upload
Custom backups need a storage account
script: To add a custom domain, create a CNAME or A record, plus a TXT record that verifies ownership.
Secure it with a free App Service managed certificate, a certificate from Key Vault, or one you upload.
App Service can back up apps automatically. Custom backups need a storage account.
For networking, VNet integration lets the app reach private resources, and a private endpoint gives the app a private inbound address.

slides.title: Scenario: release a web app with a safe rollback path
bullets: Validate the new version before users see it
Production and staging use different connection settings
Promote only after a health check
Pause and choose an App Service release feature
script: A team is updating a web app in Azure App Service. They need to validate the new version before users see it, preserve different settings for staging and production, and return to the previous version if the health check fails. Pause and choose an App Service release feature that fits.

slides.title: Solution: deployment slots with sticky settings
bullets: Deploy the candidate to a staging slot on a supported plan
Mark environment-specific settings as slot settings
Warm up and validate, then swap staging with production
If needed, swap back to the previous production version
script: Use a staging deployment slot in an App Service plan that supports slots, such as Standard or higher. Mark environment-specific settings as slot settings so they stay with their slot instead of swapping with the application content. Warm up the staging app, run the health check, and swap it into production. If validation fails after release, swap back to restore the previous production version. A slot swap is a release technique; keep backup and recovery configured separately.

slides.title: Module 3 recap
bullets: Bicep compiles to ARM; Complete mode deletes
ACR stores, ACI runs, Container Apps scales
script: Let's recap module three.
Bicep compiles to ARM JSON, and Complete mode deletes resources that aren't in the template.
Availability sets give 99.95 percent, and availability zones give 99.99 percent.
Scale sets autoscale identical VMs.
Container Registry stores images, Container Instances runs them simply, and Container Apps scales microservices.
And App Service slots and autoscale require at least the Standard tier.
Next, read the study guide or practice compute questions.

modules.title: Implement and manage virtual networking
modules.summary: Virtual networks and peering, routing, NSGs and ASGs, Bastion, service and private endpoints, Azure DNS and load balancing.

guide.html: This domain is worth 15–20% of the exam. It covers virtual networks and connectivity, secure access to virtual networks, and name resolution and load balancing.

• A virtual network (VNet) is a private network in one region and one subscription, with one or more address spaces (use private RFC 1918 ranges such as 10.0.0.0/16).
  • Subnets divide the address space. Azure reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet: the network address, the first three host addresses (gateway and DNS), and the broadcast address. A /24 gives 251 usable addresses.
  • Some services need a dedicated subnet with a specific name: GatewaySubnet for VPN/ExpressRoute gateways, AzureBastionSubnet (at least /26), AzureFirewallSubnet.
  • Public IP addresses: the Standard SKU is static, zone-redundant capable and secure by default (closed until an NSG allows traffic). Basic SKU public IPs have been retired.

Peering connects two VNets over the Microsoft backbone with low latency. It can be regional or global (different regions), and across subscriptions and tenants.

  • Address spaces must not overlap.
  • Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A can't reach C unless you peer them directly, or route through a network virtual appliance (NVA) or Azure Firewall in B.
  • A peering link is created on both sides; status should show Connected.
  • Gateway transit: the hub VNet enables Allow gateway transit and the spoke enables Use remote gateways, so spokes share the hub's VPN gateway.

Azure creates system routes automatically: traffic flows between subnets in a VNet, to peered VNets, and to the internet by default.

User-defined routes (UDRs) in a route table override system routes. A route table is associated with subnets. Common next hop types:

Next hopUse
Virtual applianceSend traffic through a firewall or NVA (give its private IP)
Virtual network gatewayForce traffic to on-premises
InternetSend to the internet
NoneDrop the traffic

The most specific prefix (longest match) wins. An NVA needs IP forwarding enabled on its network interface. Use Network Watcher Next hop or Effective routes to troubleshoot.

guide.h: Network security groups and application security groups
guide.html:
An NSG filters traffic with rules containing: priority (100–4096, lower number wins), source, destination, port, protocol, direction and allow/deny. NSGs can be associated with subnets and network interfaces.

Default rules (priority 65000+) allow VNet-to-VNet traffic and Azure Load Balancer probes, allow outbound internet, and deny all other inbound traffic.

When NSGs are on both a subnet and a NIC, both must allow the traffic. Inbound is evaluated subnet NSG first, then NIC NSG; outbound is the reverse.

Application security groups (ASGs) group VM network interfaces by role (such as WebServers) so rules can use the group instead of IP addresses.

Use effective security rules on a NIC, and Network Watcher IP flow verify, to see which rule allows or denies traffic.

• Azure Bastion gives RDP and SSH to VMs over TLS from the portal, without public IPs on the VMs. Deploy it in AzureBastionSubnet. SKUs: Developer, Basic, Standard (native client, scaling, shareable links), Premium.
  • Service endpoints extend a subnet's identity to Azure services over the backbone. The service still has its public IP; you restrict the service's firewall to the subnet. Configured on the subnet, per service.
  • Private endpoints give a specific service instance a private IP in your VNet, powered by Private Link. Works from peered VNets and on-premises too, and blocks data exfiltration to other instances. Requires DNS (a private DNS zone such as privatelink.blob.core.windows.net).

• Public DNS zones host your domain's records in Azure. Delegate the domain by updating the NS records at your registrar to Azure's name servers.
  • Record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV, NS, SOA, CAA, and alias records that point at Azure resources (like a public IP) and update automatically.
  • Private DNS zones resolve names inside VNets. Link the zone to VNets; enable auto-registration so VM records are created automatically (one auto-registration zone per VNet).
  • By default, VMs use Azure-provided DNS (168.63.129.16). You can set custom DNS servers on the VNet or NIC.

ServiceLayerScopeTypical use
Azure Load Balancer4 (TCP/UDP)RegionalDistribute traffic to VMs
Application Gateway7 (HTTP/S)RegionalURL routing, TLS termination, WAF
Azure Front Door7GlobalGlobal web apps, CDN, WAF
Traffic ManagerDNSGlobalDNS-based routing between regions

Azure Load Balancer components: frontend IP (public or internal), backend pool, health probe, load-balancing rule, and inbound NAT rules (for example, RDP to a specific VM). Session persistence can keep a client on the same backend. The Standard SKU is secure by default: you need an NSG to allow traffic to backends.

If a backend isn't receiving traffic, check the health probe and the NSG (it must allow the AzureLoadBalancer service tag).

guide.h: Worked scenario: private endpoint works by IP, not by name
guide.html:
Scenario: An app in one virtual network must reach a Storage account through a private endpoint in a peered virtual network. The endpoint is provisioned, but the app resolves the storage name to a public IP.

Pause and decide: Is the remaining problem routing, network security, or name resolution?

Recommended investigation

  1. Verify that VNet peering and the relevant network security rules allow a path to the private endpoint's IP.
  2. Check DNS from the app's network. The service name must resolve through the appropriate privatelink DNS zone to the private endpoint address.
  3. Link the private DNS zone to the client VNet, or configure the organization's DNS forwarding path to resolve that zone.
  4. Retest name resolution and connectivity. A successful IP test alone doesn't prove that application clients are using the private endpoint.

Exam distinction: Peering provides network connectivity between VNets, but the client still needs the correct DNS answer. A service endpoint keeps the service's public endpoint; a private endpoint adds a private IP for a specific service resource.

Microsoft Learn: Private endpoint DNS integration

tips: Peering is not transitive; use direct peering or a hub NVA/firewall with UDRs.
Lower NSG priority numbers are processed first.
Need a private IP for a PaaS service? Private endpoint. Just need to lock it to a subnet? Service endpoint.
Azure reserves 5 addresses per subnet.
Layer 4 → Load Balancer; HTTP path routing or WAF in one region → Application Gateway; global HTTP → Front Door.
terms: UDR
User-defined route in a route table that overrides Azure's system routes.
NVA
Network virtual appliance, such as a third-party firewall VM.
ASG
Application security group: a label for NICs used in NSG rules.
Private Link
Technology that exposes a service through a private endpoint in your VNet.
Health probe
A check the load balancer uses to decide which backends receive traffic.

slides.title: Implement and manage virtual networking
script: Welcome to module four: implementing and managing virtual networking.
This domain is worth fifteen to twenty percent of the exam.
We'll build up from virtual networks and peering, to routing and security, and finish with DNS and load balancing.

slides.title: Virtual networks and subnets
script: A virtual network is your private network in Azure. It lives in one region and one subscription.
You divide its address space into subnets.
Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet, so a slash twenty-four gives you two hundred fifty-one usable addresses.
Some services need a dedicated subnet with a specific name, such as GatewaySubnet for VPN gateways and AzureBastionSubnet for Bastion.

slides.title: Public IP addresses
bullets: Closed until an NSG allows traffic
script: Public IP addresses let resources talk to the internet.
Use the Standard SKU. It's always static, it can be zone redundant, and it's secure by default, meaning inbound traffic is blocked until a network security group allows it.
The Basic SKU has been retired, so new deployments use Standard.

slides.title: VNet peering
bullets: Connects VNets over the Microsoft backbone
script: Peering connects two virtual networks so they communicate privately over the Microsoft backbone.
It works within a region or globally, and even across subscriptions and tenants.
The address spaces must not overlap.
And the big exam point: peering is not transitive. If A is peered with B, and B with C, A can't reach C unless you peer them directly or route through a firewall in the hub.

slides.title: Hub and spoke with gateway transit
bullets: Firewall in hub + UDRs for spoke-to-spoke
script: The hub and spoke design puts shared services in a central hub VNet.
On the hub's peering, allow gateway transit. On each spoke's peering, use remote gateways. Now all spokes reach on-premises through the hub's single VPN gateway.
For spokes to talk to each other, route their traffic through a firewall or virtual appliance in the hub.

slides.title: User-defined routes
bullets: Next hop: virtual appliance, gateway, internet, none
Longest prefix wins; NVAs need IP forwarding
script: Azure creates system routes automatically, so subnets, peered networks and the internet are reachable by default.
To change that, create a route table with user-defined routes and associate it with a subnet.
The table on screen sends all internet traffic through a firewall appliance at ten dot zero dot zero dot four.
The most specific prefix wins. And the appliance's network interface must have IP forwarding enabled.

slides.title: Network security groups
bullets: Rules: priority, source, destination, port, action
script: Network security groups filter traffic using rules.
Each rule has a priority between one hundred and four thousand ninety-six. Lower numbers are processed first, and processing stops at the first match.
Default rules allow traffic within the virtual network and from the load balancer, and deny all other inbound traffic.
You can attach an NSG to a subnet, a network interface, or both.

slides.title: NSG on subnet and NIC
bullets: Inbound: subnet NSG, then NIC NSG
Outbound: NIC NSG, then subnet NSG
script: When there's an NSG on both the subnet and the network interface, traffic must be allowed by both.
Inbound traffic hits the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG. Outbound traffic goes the other way.
If traffic is blocked, look at the effective security rules on the network interface, or use IP flow verify in Network Watcher.

slides.title: Application security groups
bullets: Group NICs by role: WebServers, DbServers
Use ASGs as rule source or destination
script: Application security groups let you write NSG rules using roles instead of IP addresses.
Put your web server network interfaces in a WebServers group and your database servers in a DbServers group.
Then a rule can simply say: allow port fourteen thirty-three from WebServers to DbServers. When you add a new VM, just add it to the right group.

slides.title: Azure Bastion
bullets: RDP and SSH from the portal over TLS
script: Azure Bastion lets you connect to VMs with RDP or SSH right from the portal, over TLS.
Your VMs don't need public IP addresses, which removes a big attack surface.
Bastion is deployed into a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet that's at least a slash twenty-six.
Higher SKUs add features like native client support and scaling.

slides.title: Service vs private endpoints
bullets: Service endpoint: subnet identity, public IP remains
Private endpoint: private IP for one resource
Private endpoints work from on-premises and peered VNets
script: Service endpoints and private endpoints both keep traffic to Azure services on the Microsoft backbone, but they work differently.
A service endpoint extends your subnet's identity to a service like Storage. The service keeps its public IP, but its firewall can allow only your subnet.
A private endpoint gives one specific resource a private IP address inside your virtual network. It works from peered networks and on-premises, and needs a private DNS zone for name resolution.

slides.title: Azure DNS
script: Azure DNS hosts public zones. To make Azure answer for your domain, update the name server records at your registrar.
Alias records point at Azure resources, like a public IP, and update automatically if the address changes.
Private DNS zones resolve names inside virtual networks. Link the zone to each virtual network, and turn on auto-registration so VM records are created for you.

slides.title: Choosing a load balancer
script: Azure has four load-balancing services.
Azure Load Balancer works at layer four for TCP and UDP within a region.
Application Gateway works at layer seven, with URL path routing, TLS termination and a web application firewall.
Front Door is the global layer seven option, and Traffic Manager routes globally using DNS.
The AZ-104 exam focuses most on Azure Load Balancer.

slides.title: Azure Load Balancer parts
script: A load balancer has a frontend IP address, which can be public or internal.
Load-balancing rules map frontend ports to a backend pool of VMs or a scale set.
Health probes decide which backends receive traffic, and inbound NAT rules forward a port to one specific VM.
If a backend gets no traffic, check the health probe, and make sure its NSG allows the AzureLoadBalancer service tag.

slides.title: Scenario: a private endpoint resolves to a public IP
bullets: An app VNet is peered with the VNet hosting a Storage private endpoint
The endpoint is provisioned and network rules allow the path
The app's storage hostname still resolves to a public IP
Pause and identify the next thing to troubleshoot
script: An application is in one virtual network. A Storage private endpoint is in a peered virtual network, and the network path is allowed. Yet the application resolves the storage hostname to a public IP. Pause and decide whether to change the route, the network security rule, or DNS.

slides.title: Solution: resolve the service name to the private endpoint
bullets: Check connectivity and NSG rules to the private endpoint IP
Resolve the service hostname through its private-link DNS zone
Link the zone to the client VNet or configure DNS forwarding
script: When an application hostname resolves to a public IP, check DNS before changing a route that is already allowed. Configure the appropriate private-link DNS zone and make it resolvable from the client VNet. That can mean linking the zone to the VNet or configuring the existing DNS forwarding design. Then verify the hostname returns the private endpoint address and retest the application. Peering carries traffic; it doesn't by itself supply the correct private DNS answer.

slides.title: Module 4 recap
bullets: UDRs steer traffic; NVAs need IP forwarding
Lower NSG priority wins; both NSGs must allow
Private endpoint = private IP for a service
script: Let's recap module four.
Azure reserves five IP addresses per subnet.
Peering isn't transitive.
User-defined routes steer traffic, and appliances need IP forwarding.
In NSGs, lower priority numbers win, and when there are two NSGs, both must allow the traffic.
And a private endpoint gives a service a private IP in your network.
Next, read the study guide or practice networking questions.

modules.title: Monitor and maintain Azure resources
modules.summary: Azure Monitor metrics, logs and KQL, alerts and action groups, Insights and Network Watcher, plus Azure Backup and Site Recovery.

guide.html: This domain is worth 10–15% of the exam. It has two parts: monitoring resources with Azure Monitor, and backup and recovery with Azure Backup and Azure Site Recovery.

guide.h: Azure Monitor data: metrics and logs
guide.html:
MetricsLogs
WhatNumeric values at regular intervalsRecords with many properties (events, traces)
StoreTime-series database, kept 93 daysLog Analytics workspace
Explore withMetrics explorerLog Analytics with KQL
Good forNear real-time alerting and chartsDeep analysis and correlation
  • Platform metrics are collected automatically. The activity log records subscription-level control-plane events (who created or deleted what) and is kept for 90 days.
  • Diagnostic settings send resource logs and metrics to a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account (archive) or an event hub (streaming).
  • Guest OS data from VMs is collected by the Azure Monitor Agent using data collection rules (DCRs). (The older Log Analytics agent is retired.)

Kusto Query Language (KQL) pipes a table through operators:

Perf
| where ObjectName == "Processor" and CounterName == "% Processor Time"
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize avg(CounterValue) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| render timechart

Common operators: where (filter), project (choose columns), summarize (aggregate), count, top/order by, extend (add a computed column), join, and render (chart). Common tables: Heartbeat, Perf, Event, Syslog, AzureActivity, AzureDiagnostics.

• Alert rules define a scope (resources), a condition (signal + logic) and actions. Signal types: metric, log search, activity log (including Service Health and Resource Health), and others.
  • Action groups are reusable lists of notifications (email, SMS, push, voice) and actions (Azure Functions, Logic Apps, Automation runbooks, webhooks, ITSM, Event Hubs). One action group can serve many alert rules.
  • Alert processing rules modify fired alerts: suppress notifications during maintenance windows, or add action groups to many alerts at once.
  • Severity ranges from Sev 0 (critical) to Sev 4 (verbose).
  • Service Health alerts tell you about Azure outages, planned maintenance and advisories affecting your subscriptions.

Insights are curated monitoring experiences: VM insights (performance and dependency maps), Container insights, Storage insights, Network insights and Application Insights (application performance monitoring).

Azure Network Watcher tools:

ToolAnswers
IP flow verifyIs a packet allowed or denied, and by which NSG rule?
Next hopWhere does traffic to this IP go next? Which route table?
Connection troubleshootCan this VM reach that endpoint, and where does it fail?
Connection monitorOngoing reachability and latency between endpoints
Packet captureCapture traffic to and from a VM
Flow logsRecord IP traffic through NSGs or VNets (VNet flow logs replace NSG flow logs)
TopologyVisual map of network resources

Backups are stored in a vault:

VaultProtects
Recovery Services vaultAzure VMs, SQL Server and SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, on-premises (MARS agent, MABS/DPM); also used by Site Recovery
Backup vaultNewer workloads: Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, AKS
  • A backup policy sets the schedule and retention (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly). Enhanced VM policies allow multiple backups per day.
  • The vault must be in the same region as the VMs it protects.
  • Storage redundancy for the vault (LRS, ZRS, GRS) must be set before protecting the first item. GRS enables optional Cross Region Restore.
  • Restore options for VMs: create a new VM, restore disks, replace existing disks, or file-level recovery (mount a recovery point and copy files).
  • Soft delete keeps deleted backup data for 14 days by default. Immutable vaults and multi-user authorization protect against malicious deletion.
  • Monitor with Backup center (Business Continuity Center), backup reports and alerts.

Site Recovery replicates VMs continuously to a secondary region (or from on-premises to Azure) so you can fail over during an outage.

  • Uses a Recovery Services vault in the target (secondary) region.
  • Recovery plans group machines and order failover steps, with scripts and manual actions.
  • Test failover runs into an isolated network without affecting production replication.
  • Failover types: planned (no data loss) and unplanned. After failover, commit, then re-protect to replicate back, and fail back later.
  • Backup = point-in-time copies for restore (RPO in hours/days); Site Recovery = disaster recovery with low RPO and RTO (minutes).

guide.h: Worked scenario: alert on CPU without maintenance noise
guide.html:
Scenario: A team wants to know when a VM's CPU exceeds a threshold. The signal is numeric and available as a platform metric. Planned maintenance happens every Saturday night, when notifications should be suppressed.

Pause and decide: Which alert type matches the signal, and what should change during the maintenance window?

Recommended design

  1. Create a metric alert rule scoped to the VM and configure the CPU condition and evaluation settings.
  2. Attach an action group for the required notifications or automation.
  3. Create a scheduled alert processing rule to suppress the action group during the maintenance window.
  4. After the window, confirm the processing rule schedule and alert action behavior are back to normal.

Exam distinction: Metric alerts evaluate numeric metric signals. Log search alerts evaluate a Log Analytics query. Alert processing rules modify or suppress actions for triggered alerts; they are useful for planned notification windows without deleting the alert rule.

Microsoft Learn: Azure Monitor alerts

tips: Need ongoing alerts on a numeric value in near real time? A metric alert. Complex conditions over log data? A log search alert.
Silence alerts during a maintenance window with an alert processing rule, not by deleting rules.
Which NSG rule blocks a packet? IP flow verify. Which route is used? Next hop.
Recovery Services vaults must be in the same region as the protected VMs.
Change vault redundancy before you back up anything.
terms: Log Analytics workspace
The store for Azure Monitor logs, queried with KQL.
Data collection rule
Defines what the Azure Monitor Agent collects and where it sends it.
Action group
A reusable set of notifications and automated actions triggered by alerts.
RPO / RTO
Recovery point objective (how much data you can lose) and recovery time objective (how long recovery can take).
Re-protect
After failover, start replicating from the new primary back to the original region.

slides.title: Monitor and maintain Azure resources
bullets: Azure Monitor: metrics, logs and KQL
Alerts, action groups, Insights and Network Watcher
script: Welcome to module five: monitoring and maintaining Azure resources.
This domain is worth ten to fifteen percent of the exam.
We'll cover Azure Monitor data, alerting, troubleshooting tools, and how to protect workloads with Azure Backup and Site Recovery.

slides.title: Metrics vs logs
bullets: Activity log: who did what, 90 days
script: Azure Monitor collects two main kinds of data.
Metrics are numeric values sampled at regular intervals, like CPU percentage. They're lightweight, near real-time and kept for ninety-three days.
Logs are rich records stored in a Log Analytics workspace and queried with the Kusto Query Language.
The activity log is a special log that records control-plane operations, like who deleted a resource. It's kept for ninety days.

slides.title: Getting data where you need it
bullets: Destinations: Log Analytics, storage, Event Hubs
Azure Monitor Agent + data collection rules for VMs
script: Resource logs aren't stored anywhere until you create a diagnostic setting.
A diagnostic setting sends logs and metrics to a Log Analytics workspace for analysis, a storage account for cheap archiving, or an event hub for streaming to other tools.
For data from inside a VM's operating system, install the Azure Monitor Agent and define a data collection rule describing what to collect.

slides.title: KQL basics
bullets: Start with a table, pipe through operators
Common tables: Heartbeat, Perf, Event, AzureActivity

visual.text:
Perf
| where CounterName == "% Processor Time"
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize avg(CounterValue) by Computer
| order by avg_CounterValue desc

script: Kusto queries start with a table and pipe the data through operators.
This example starts with the Perf table, filters to processor time in the last hour, and calculates the average per computer.
The operators to know are where for filtering, project for choosing columns, summarize for aggregating, and render for charts.
You'll often see tables like Heartbeat, Perf, Event and AzureActivity.

slides.title: Alert rules
bullets: Service Health alerts for Azure outages
script: An alert rule watches a scope of resources for a condition, and runs actions when it fires.
Use a metric alert for numeric thresholds in near real time, a log search alert for conditions over log data, and an activity log alert for events such as a resource being deleted.
Severity runs from zero, critical, to four, verbose.
Service Health alerts notify you about Azure outages and planned maintenance.

slides.title: Action groups
bullets: Act: Functions, Logic Apps, runbooks, webhooks

items.d: Email, SMS, Azure app push, voice
Automation runbook, Function, Logic App, webhook

script: An action group is a reusable list of who to notify and what to run.
Notifications include email, SMS, push to the Azure mobile app, and voice calls.
Actions can run an Automation runbook, an Azure Function, a Logic App or a webhook.
Because they're reusable, one action group can serve dozens of alert rules.

slides.title: Alert processing rules
bullets: Scope by subscription, resource group or resource
script: Alert processing rules change what happens after alerts fire.
The classic use is a maintenance window: suppress notifications every Saturday night without disabling your alert rules.
They can also add an action group to all alerts in a subscription or resource group, so you don't have to edit each rule.

slides.title: Insights
script: Insights are ready-made monitoring experiences.
VM insights shows performance charts and a map of the processes and connections on your VMs.
There are also insights for containers, storage accounts and networks.
And Application Insights monitors application performance, failures and usage.

slides.title: Network Watcher

head: Question
Tool
rows: Is traffic going to my firewall?
Can VM1 reach the SQL server?

script: Network Watcher is your toolbox for network problems.
IP flow verify tells you whether a packet is allowed or denied, and which NSG rule decided it.
Next hop tells you where traffic goes next and which route table is responsible.
Connection troubleshoot tests reachability between a VM and an endpoint, and connection monitor watches it continuously.
Packet capture and flow logs record the traffic itself.

slides.title: Two kinds of vault
bullets: Recovery Services vault: VMs, SQL in VMs, Azure Files, on-premises, Site Recovery
Same region as the protected resources

items.d: Azure VMs, Azure Files, SQL/SAP HANA in VMs, MARS

script: Azure Backup stores data in one of two vault types.
The Recovery Services vault protects Azure VMs, SQL Server and SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises machines. Site Recovery uses it too.
The Backup vault protects newer workloads, like managed disks, blobs, PostgreSQL and Kubernetes.
A vault must be in the same region as the resources it backs up.

slides.title: Backup policies and restores
bullets: Restore a new VM, disks, or replace disks
script: A backup policy defines when backups run and how long recovery points are kept.
Set the vault's storage redundancy before you protect anything, because it generally can't be changed once items are protected. Geo-redundant storage also enables cross region restore.
You can restore a whole new VM, restore or replace disks, or use file-level recovery to mount a recovery point and copy individual files.

slides.title: Protecting your backups
script: Backups are a target for attackers, so protect them.
Soft delete keeps deleted backup data for fourteen days by default.
Immutable vaults prevent recovery points from being deleted before they expire.
Multi-user authorization requires a second person to approve critical operations.
Monitor everything from Backup center, also called the Business Continuity Center.

slides.title: Azure Site Recovery
script: Azure Site Recovery provides disaster recovery.
It continuously replicates VMs to a secondary region, using a Recovery Services vault in that target region.
Recovery plans group machines and order the failover steps.
Run a test failover into an isolated network to prove it works without touching production.
After a real failover, commit, re-protect to replicate back, and fail back when the primary region is healthy.

slides.title: Backup vs Site Recovery
bullets: Site Recovery: keep apps running in another region
Low RPO and RTO with Site Recovery
script: Backup and Site Recovery solve different problems.
Backup keeps point-in-time copies so you can recover data after deletion or corruption.
Site Recovery keeps the whole application ready to run in another region, with a recovery point objective of seconds to minutes.
Most organizations use both.

slides.title: Scenario: CPU alerts during a maintenance window
bullets: A VM's CPU metric needs a threshold alert
Notify the operations team when it fires
Suppress notifications during scheduled Saturday maintenance
Pause and choose the alert and maintenance controls
script: A team needs a notification when a virtual machine's CPU metric crosses a threshold. During scheduled Saturday maintenance, the notification should be suppressed. Pause and choose the alert type, notification action, and maintenance control.

slides.title: Solution: metric alert, action group, processing rule
bullets: Use a metric alert for the VM's CPU signal
Attach an action group for notifications or automation
Schedule an alert processing rule to suppress actions during maintenance
Keep the alert rule so monitoring resumes after the window
script: CPU is a numeric platform metric, so create a metric alert rule for the VM and define the threshold and evaluation behavior. Attach an action group for the operations team's notification or automation. Use a scheduled alert processing rule to suppress the action group during the maintenance window. Keep the alert rule in place so the same monitoring can notify the team outside the scheduled suppression period. A log search alert would be the better fit for a condition that must be evaluated from Log Analytics query results.

slides.title: Module 5 recap
bullets: Metrics for fast alerts, logs for analysis
Action groups are reusable; processing rules suppress
IP flow verify and next hop troubleshoot networks
Vault in the same region; Site Recovery for DR
script: Let's recap module five.
Metrics are great for fast alerts, and logs for deep analysis with KQL.
Diagnostic settings route resource logs to a workspace, storage or event hub.
Action groups are reusable, and alert processing rules can suppress notifications.
IP flow verify and next hop troubleshoot network issues.
And for protection, keep the backup vault in the same region, and use Site Recovery for disaster recovery.
